summary: A perennial tussock grass with sugary young leaf tissue above recessed growing points, silica-bearing mature blades and deep fibrous roots. Falling root-zone water triggers leaf rolling, growth arrest and foliage loss on drained eastern meadow patches; wetter spring margins can remain green. It is rondo's principal green-season grass staple, with a summer forage gap buffered partly by dried-fruit caches carried in its paired gular pouch. Wind carries pollen and seeds, and tall unbrowsed margins conceal garfio (F8, F9, F18, F26).

chains.trait: Drought-triggered growth arrest above protected basal buds
links: On drained eastern meadow soils, summer water loss can exceed rain and fog recharge; dawn surface wetting does not necessarily replenish the deeper root zone.
Declining root-zone water triggers stomatal restriction and longitudinal leaf rolling, sheltering stomata within a more humid leaf microclimate.
Continued water shortage arrests new leaf production and promotes loss of older foliage, reducing demand while recessed buds remain protected by persistent sheaths.
Reduced demand and stored reserves prolong meristem survival through the deficit, allowing surviving crowns to resume growth after sustained root-zone rewetting.
chains.play: Read rolled leaves and straw-coloured foliage as local water-stress signals; compare dry slopes with green spring margins and revisit surviving crowns after sustained rain.
chains.weakness: Repeated grazing before reserves recover, crown damage or drought beyond the roots' remaining water access can kill a tussock; fog alone may not end the stress.
observe: Blades roll as the soil beneath them dries, even when dawn fog briefly wets their surfaces.
Dry-slope clumps lose green foliage while crowns beside a persistent seep remain active.
New leaves emerge from surviving crowns after the root zone is thoroughly rewetted.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: Dawn fog does not guarantee adequate summer root-zone water. Seasonal dormancy is distinct from temporary wilting, and regrowth requires viable buds and sufficient reserves; fire is not a reproductive trigger. Strict review (2026-11-19): revised: The original chain left its cue undefined; the rewrite makes arrest water-triggered, separates rolling from growth arrest and states meristem survival as the payoff. Residual: F18 explicitly establishes summer drying and F8 does not guarantee root-zone recharge, so the water-deficit premise holds. Reduced transpiration, foliage loss and surviving basal buds can support recovery without invoking fire or programmed dormancy. Residual weakness: leaf rolling conserves water only insofar as its geometry shelters stomatal surfaces, and recessed buds protect against removal more directly than against dehydration. The stated limits on residual water access, reserve depletion and crown survival prevent an unsupported guarantee of drought survival.

analogues.mechanism: Leaf rolling, reduced growth, foliage loss and protected basal meristems provide a drought-survival analogy. This rewrite uses water-triggered quiescence rather than claiming an independently programmed summer dormancy.

chains.trait: Protected growing points beneath accessible young leaves and silicified older tissue
links: Repeated rondo grazing removes accessible young leaves, favouring crowns whose buds and leaf-growth zones remain recessed within basal sheaths below the usual bite height.
Roots take up dissolved silicon where weathering of volcanic silicates and soil water make it available, depositing some in maturing blades and outer sheaths.
Sugary young leaf portions remain accessible above the protected crown; older silicified tissue adds partial abrasion resistance without making the growing points the required feeding target.
Light grazing leaves recessed meristems and sufficient reserves intact, allowing replacement leaves to grow; crown excavation defeats this tolerance mechanism.
chains.play: Cut a few soft young leaf portions at least 5 cm above the visible crown for food or a rondo gift; leave basal sheaths and whole tillers attached.
chains.weakness: Silica protection is partial and depends on dissolved supply; repeated defoliation exhausts reserves, while pulling tillers or excavating the crown can remove growing points.
observe: Mature blades have rough margins while accessible young leaf portions remain soft above the crown.
Rondo crops leaves above the persistent basal sheaths without routinely digging into them.
Lightly cropped crowns produce replacement leaves, while uprooted or excavated crowns leave damaged gaps.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: Silica is a physical feeding deterrent, not an alkaloid or a wind-resistance mechanism. The analogue demonstrates effects on insect folivores; rondo's selective grazing is a fictional ecological extension. Strict review (2026-11-19): revised: The original defence directed feeding toward vulnerable bases; the rewrite places edible tissue above protected growing points and treats silica as a conditional secondary contribution. Residual: Protected basal growth zones provide a coherent grazing-tolerance mechanism independently of silica. F7 and F9 establish volcanic parent material, but do not quantify plant-available silicon; F23 concerns animal mineral resources rather than silicon uptake. The rewrite appropriately makes silicification conditional on dissolved supply. F26 supports sugary food, while rondo's documented grass diet supplies the actual herbivore link. Residual uncertainty is the distribution of silicification and its effect on rondo; neither is required to explain regrowth after light grazing.

analogues.mechanism: Protected basal growth zones support grazing tolerance. The supplied insect-feeding analogue supports possible effects of silica on herbivores, but their strength varies and does not establish reduced feeding quality for rondo; crown survival and regrowth provide the principal mechanism here.

food_for: rondo grazes accessible young leaves during green growth.
zancuda takes soft leaves along damp meadow margins.
player_lineage gathers sugary young leaf portions above the crown.
babosa consumes decaying litter in damp tussock bases.
gameplay.gift_item: A small bundle of soft young leaf portions for rondo, cut at least 5 cm above the visible crown.

poison.signal: Ordinary green growth and straw-coloured drought foliage; rough mature blades indicate silicified tissue.

gameplay.cover: Dense, tall, unbrowsed margins conceal small bodies and interrupt sightlines; cropped lawns and sparse drought clumps offer little concealment.
gameplay.notes: Harvest accessible soft leaf portions without pulling whole tillers or cutting basal sheaths. The 5 cm cutting rule is a conservative gameplay clearance above the crown. Light harvest permits recovery only while water and reserves suffice. Rondo's dried-fruit caches partly buffer seasonal loss of green forage. Silica-bearing foliage is neither a medicinal mineral source nor a substitute for salt.

relations.note: The principal green-season grass staple; rondo crops young leaves above persistent crowns, while dried-fruit caches partly buffer the drought forage gap.
Tall ungrazed margins conceal short approach routes toward rondo feeding patches; cropped or sparse drought patches provide little cover.
Takes soft leaves along damp meadow margins.
Consumes decaying litter in sufficiently damp tussock bases.
Grass gives way to riparian shrub strips where channels retain water through meadow drought.
Harvests accessible young leaf portions above the crown; pulling tillers or excavating bases damages recovery.

generator.trunk: No woody trunk; clustered tillers arise from a persistent basal crown with recessed buds and leaf-growth zones inside protective sheaths.

branching.buttress: Absent; generate basal tillers rather than hierarchical branches.

leaf.type: Long narrow blade with rough mature margins and reversible longitudinal rolling
leaf.arrangement: Alternate two-ranked leaves on clustered tillers. Treat size_cm as the green-state nominal length: use 15–45 cm on intact growing clumps, reserving 45 cm for tall culms; shorten surviving blades to fit cropped states.

overlay_rules: Accessible young leaf portions are pale green above the crown.
Water-stressed foliage rolls and becomes muted straw-gold as it senesces.
Dry outer sheaths persist around living crowns.
Cropped green patches expose short leaf tips and coarse basal sheaths.

placement.slope: Valley floors, gentle eastern slopes and sheltered meadow benches.
placement.wetness: Seasonally moist root zones followed by local summer drying; maintain active green patches where springs or seepage sustain root water.
placement.soil: Drained volcanic loam with sufficient depth for fibrous roots; dissolved silicon supply depends on weathering and water availability.
placement.fog: Frequent dawn fog, especially within the eastern valley trap; surface wetting does not automatically reset root-zone drought.
placement.density: Generate green unbrowsed stands at 0.3–1.2 m, cropped feeding routes at 0.08–0.25 m, and drought clumps with sparse living foliage beneath standing dead straw. Substantial concealment requires dense, tall, unbrowsed foliage.

generator.seasonal: Moist conditions support growth and wind-borne reproduction. Sustained root-zone drying triggers growth arrest and foliage loss; surviving crowns resume growth after sustained rewetting. Grazing height varies independently of season.
generator.wind_response: Blades and flowering stems stream with gusts; crowns remain low and tightly rooted.

journal.en: The sweet part grows low. Summer takes the green, but leaves the heart.
journal.es: Lo dulce crece abajo. El verano se lleva el verde, pero deja el corazón.

observe: Rondo grazing creates low green lawns beside taller coarse clumps.
Wind releases pollen from exposed flowering stems.
Dead outer blades shelter living basal buds during summer.
Brief dew wetting can brighten dry blades without ending dormancy.
secrets: A straw-coloured tussock with a firm living base can recover; colour alone does not reveal its condition.
Repeatedly clipped paths mark rondo feeding circuits and places where garfio may wait.
The best thatch comes from detached outer leaves, allowing the living crown to remain intact.
